# Model and source

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Nayak_2026_marstacimab"))$reference`
* Description: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Nayak_2026_marstacimab"))$description`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1007/s40262-026-01695-5> (open access; the
  supplementary appendix holds the IIV, residual-error, covariate and Emax
  equations)

Marstacimab is a human IgG1 monoclonal antibody against the Kunitz-2 domain of
tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI), given subcutaneously once weekly for
prophylaxis in hemophilia A or B. The final model (Fig. 1 of the paper) is a
two-compartment target-mediated drug disposition (TMDD) model with the
quasi-steady-state (QSS) approximation. Free drug is cleared by a linear
clearance and by an additional Michaelis-Menten pathway, and soluble TFPI is
synthesised at a constant rate, degraded as free TFPI (`kdeg`) and eliminated as
the marstacimab-TFPI complex (`kcom`). Total marstacimab and total TFPI were
both fitted. A sequential sigmoid Emax model then relates the model-predicted
free TFPI to peak thrombin from the thrombin generation assay (TGA), in
participants with hemophilia only.

# Population

The analysis pooled 213 male participants from six studies (Table 1 of the
paper): 63 healthy volunteers (phase I studies NCT02531815 and NCT04832139) and
150 participants with hemophilia (phase I NCT04878731 in China, phase Ib/II
NCT02974855, its phase II extension NCT03363321, and the non-inhibitor cohort of
phase III NCT03938792). Of the participants with hemophilia, 121 had severe
hemophilia A and 29 moderately severe to severe hemophilia B; 19 were
adolescents aged 13 to 17 years. Median (range) age was 33 (13-66) years and
median (range) body weight 71.1 (35-120) kg (Table 3). By race, 33.3% were
White, 32.4% Asian, 26.3% Native Hawaiian and 7.5% Black (Table 4); 23.6% were
ADA positive and 21.6% had mild renal impairment. Doses ranged from 30 to
450 mg SC, single or once weekly, plus 150 and 440 mg IV single doses in
healthy volunteers. The phase III regimen was a 300 mg SC loading dose followed
by 150 mg SC once weekly (QW), with escalation to 300 mg QW allowed.

The same information is available programmatically via
`readModelDb("Nayak_2026_marstacimab")()$population`.

# Source trace

Each `ini()` value carries a comment in
`inst/modeldb/specificDrugs/Nayak_2026_marstacimab.R` naming its source; the
table below collects them.

| Equation / parameter | Value | Source location |
|----------------------|-------|-----------------|
| `lcl` (CL) | 0.0188 L/h | Table 5 |
| `lvc` (Vc) | 3.61 L | Table 5 |
| `lq` (Q) | 0.00489 L/h | Table 5 |
| `lvp` (Vp) | 4.99 L | Table 5 |
| `lvmax` (Vmax, nonlinear drug clearance) | 0.53 nM/h | Table 5 |
| `lkm` (Km, nonlinear drug clearance) | 4.31 nM | Table 5 |
| `lfdepot` (F) | 0.705 | Table 5 |
| `lka` (ka) | 0.00742 1/h | Table 5 |
| `ltlag` (lag time) | 2 h | Table 5 |
| `lrbase_target` (baseline total TFPI) | 3.75 nM | Table 5 |
| `lkdeg` (kdeg, free TFPI) | 0.0161 1/h | Table 5 |
| `lkint` (kcom, complex) | 0.000754 1/h | Table 5 |
| `lkss` (KSS) | 72.2 nM | Table 5 |
| `e_wt_cl_q` | 1.14 | Table 5 (weight exponent on CL); also applied to Q, see Assumptions |
| `e_wt_vc_vp` | 1.86 | Table 5 (weight exponent on Vc); also applied to Vp, see Assumptions |
| `e_dis_healthy_cl` | 0.199 | Table 5 |
| `e_race_asian_cl` | 0.346 | Table 5 |
| `e_ada_pos_cl` | 0.229 | Table 5 |
| `e_renalimp_mild_cl` | -0.168 | Table 5 |
| `e_dis_hemophilia_b_cl` | 0.118 | Table 5 |
| `le0` (PBASE) | 37.8 nM | Table 8 |
| `lrmax_peak_thrombin` (PMAX) | 91.4 nM | Table 8 |
| `lec50` (EC50) | 2.92 nM | Table 8 |
| `hill` | 5 (fixed) | Table 8 |
| IIV variances, CL-Vc correlation -0.527 | see model file | Table 5 (PK), Table 8 (PD) |
| `expSd`, `expSd_total_target` | 0.392, 0.158 | Table 5 (additive on the log scale) |
| `addSd_peak_thrombin` | 26.3 nM | Table 8 |
| `exp(eta)` IIV on every parameter | n/a | Supplementary eq 1 |
| Log-scale residual error, `ln(Y) = ln(F) + W * eps` | n/a | Supplementary eq 3 |
| Peak thrombin `PBASE + (PMAX - PBASE) / (1 + (FTFPI / EC50)^HILL)` | n/a | Supplementary eq 5 |
| Categorical covariates `COV = 1 + theta * f` | n/a | Supplementary eq 7.1-7.2 |
| Weight `(WT / 71.1)^thetaWT` | n/a | Supplementary eq 8.1-8.2; 71.1 kg is the median of Table 3 |
| TMDD-QSS structure, nonlinear clearance of free drug | n/a | Fig. 1; Methods 'PopPK Model' |
| Marstacimab molecular weight 146 kDa | n/a | Hympavzi US prescribing information, section 11 (not stated in the paper) |

The QSS equations follow the standard Gibbiansky form. With total drug
`Ctot = central / Vc` and total TFPI `Rtot`, both in nM, free drug is
`C = 0.5 * ((Ctot - Rtot - KSS) + sqrt((Ctot - Rtot - KSS)^2 + 4 * KSS * Ctot))`.
The complex is `Ctot - C`, and free TFPI is `Rtot - (Ctot - C)`. Linear,
inter-compartmental and Michaelis-Menten fluxes act on free drug, and the
complex is eliminated at `kcom`.

# Structural checks

These checks use typical values (no random effects) and assert on
model-internal identities, so they are deterministic.

```{r structural-checks}
mod <- readModelDb("Nayak_2026_marstacimab")
mod_typ <- rxode2::zeroRe(mod)

covs_ref <- data.frame(
  WT = 71.1, DIS_HEALTHY = 0, RACE_ASIAN = 0, ADA_POS = 0,
  RENALIMP_MILD = 0, DIS_HEMOPHILIA_B = 0
)

# The model has three `~` endpoints, so observation rows carry an ODE-state
# cmt plus dvid; a forward solve returns every endpoint column regardless.
make_events <- function(id, dose_time, dose_amt, dose_cmt, obs_time, covs) {
  doses <- data.frame(
    id = id, time = dose_time, amt = dose_amt, evid = 1L,
    cmt = dose_cmt, dvid = NA_integer_
  )
  obs <- data.frame(
    id = id, time = obs_time, amt = 0, evid = 0L,
    cmt = "central", dvid = 1L
  )
  ev <- dplyr::bind_rows(doses, obs)
  ev <- ev[order(ev$time, -ev$evid), ]
  cbind(ev, covs[rep(1, nrow(ev)), , drop = FALSE], row.names = NULL)
}

# 1. Without drug, total TFPI holds at its baseline and free TFPI equals it.
ev_nodose <- make_events(1, 0, 0, "depot", c(0, 168, 1344), covs_ref)
sim_nodose <- as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(mod_typ, ev_nodose))
peak_at_baseline <- 37.8 + (91.4 - 37.8) / (1 + (3.75 / 2.92)^5)
stopifnot(
  max(abs(sim_nodose$total_target - 3.75)) < 1e-6,
  max(abs(sim_nodose$free_target - 3.75)) < 1e-6,
  max(abs(sim_nodose$peak_thrombin - peak_at_baseline)) < 1e-6
)

# 2. Immediately after a 440 mg IV bolus to a 71.1 kg healthy volunteer,
#    total concentration is dose / Vc (ug/mL = mg/L).
ev_iv <- make_events(
  1, 0, 440, "central", c(0.001, 24, 168, 672),
  transform(covs_ref, DIS_HEALTHY = 1)
)
sim_iv <- as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(mod_typ, ev_iv))
stopifnot(abs(sim_iv$Cc[1] / (440 / 3.61) - 1) < 0.01)
sim_iv[, c("time", "Cc", "total_target", "free_target")]
```

Before dosing, the predicted peak thrombin for a participant with hemophilia is
`r round(peak_at_baseline, 1)` nM. Because PBASE is the response at saturating
free TFPI, the drug-free value lies above PBASE: baseline free TFPI (3.75 nM)
is already close to EC50 (2.92 nM).

# Peak thrombin versus free TFPI (Figure 4)

Figure 4 of the paper plots peak thrombin against model-predicted free TFPI in
ng/mL, with the population Emax curve in blue. The maintainers digitised that
curve. To convert the model's nM to the figure's ng/mL they used 35.3 ng/mL per
nM, the ratio of the paper's mean baseline total TFPI (132.5 ng/mL, Table 3) to
the model's baseline total TFPI (3.75 nM, Table 5). The figure's half-maximal
point lies at about 102 ng/mL, i.e. 2.9 nM, which confirms both this factor and
the Table 8 EC50.

```{r figure-4}
ng_per_nm_tfpi <- 132.5 / 3.75
fig4_digitised <- data.frame(
  free_tfpi_ngml = c(47.7, 64, 80.4, 96.7, 113.1, 129.4, 145.8, 162.1, 178.5, 194.8, 219.3),
  peak_thrombin = c(94.3, 89.2, 80, 67.8, 57.3, 50, 45.7, 43.5, 41.9, 41.1, 40.3)
)
emax_curve <- function(free_nm) 37.8 + (91.4 - 37.8) / (1 + (free_nm / 2.92)^5)
fig4_digitised$model <- emax_curve(fig4_digitised$free_tfpi_ngml / ng_per_nm_tfpi)
fig4_digitised$pct_diff <- 100 * (fig4_digitised$model / fig4_digitised$peak_thrombin - 1)

# The plateaus of the printed curve sit about 4% above Table 8's PBASE and PMAX
# (see Assumptions); a mis-transcribed EC50, Hill or plateau moves this far more.
stopifnot(max(abs(fig4_digitised$pct_diff)) < 10)

curve_df <- data.frame(free_tfpi_ngml = seq(45, 225, by = 1))
curve_df$peak_thrombin <- emax_curve(curve_df$free_tfpi_ngml / ng_per_nm_tfpi)

ggplot(curve_df, aes(free_tfpi_ngml, peak_thrombin)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = fig4_digitised, shape = 21, size = 2) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 120)) +
  labs(
    x = "Free TFPI (ng/mL)", y = "Peak thrombin (nM)",
    title = "Peak thrombin vs free TFPI, typical values",
    caption = "Line: Table 8 parameters. Points: curve digitised from Figure 4 of Nayak 2026."
  )

knitr::kable(fig4_digitised, digits = 1,
  caption = "Digitised Figure 4 curve vs the Table 8 Emax equation.")
```

# Virtual cohort

Table 7 of the paper summarises steady-state exposure from the empirical Bayes
estimates of the participants with hemophilia, simulated on 150 mg or 300 mg SC
QW. The virtual cohorts below approximate those participants. Covariate
proportions are computed from Table 4. Adults have 43.5% Asian, 19% hemophilia
B, 20.6% ADA positive and 16% mild renal impairment. Adolescents have 36.8%
Asian, 21% hemophilia B, 10.5% ADA positive and no renal impairment. Body
weight is drawn from a normal distribution truncated to the observed range,
using the Table 3 phase III moments: adults 71.6 (SD 15.6) kg, 43.2-120 kg, and
adolescents 54.7 (SD 12.8) kg, 35-74.1 kg. The 300 mg adolescent group of
Table 7 had two participants and is not simulated.

```{r cohort}
set.seed(20261123)
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20261123)

n_per_arm <- 200
tau <- 168
n_doses <- 30
ss_start <- (n_doses - 1) * tau

draw_truncnorm <- function(n, mean, sd, lower, upper) {
  x <- rnorm(n, mean, sd)
  bad <- x < lower | x > upper
  while (any(bad)) {
    x[bad] <- rnorm(sum(bad), mean, sd)
    bad <- x < lower | x > upper
  }
  x
}

make_cohort <- function(n, cohort, dose, wt, p_asian, p_hb, p_ada, p_renal, id_offset) {
  subj <- data.frame(
    id = id_offset + seq_len(n),
    cohort = cohort,
    WT = draw_truncnorm(n, wt[1], wt[2], wt[3], wt[4]),
    DIS_HEALTHY = 0L,
    RACE_ASIAN = rbinom(n, 1, p_asian),
    DIS_HEMOPHILIA_B = rbinom(n, 1, p_hb),
    ADA_POS = rbinom(n, 1, p_ada),
    RENALIMP_MILD = rbinom(n, 1, p_renal)
  )
  obs_time <- sort(unique(c(
    seq(0, n_doses * tau, by = 24),
    seq(0, tau, by = 6),
    seq(ss_start, ss_start + tau, by = 6)
  )))
  doses <- tidyr::crossing(subj, time = (seq_len(n_doses) - 1) * tau) |>
    dplyr::mutate(amt = dose, evid = 1L, cmt = "depot", dvid = NA_integer_)
  obs <- tidyr::crossing(subj, time = obs_time) |>
    dplyr::mutate(amt = 0, evid = 0L, cmt = "central", dvid = 1L)
  dplyr::bind_rows(doses, obs) |>
    dplyr::arrange(id, time, dplyr::desc(evid))
}

events <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  make_cohort(n_per_arm, "150 mg (adults)", 150, c(71.6, 15.6, 43.2, 120),
              0.435, 0.19, 0.206, 0.16, id_offset = 0L),
  make_cohort(n_per_arm, "300 mg (adults)", 300, c(71.6, 15.6, 43.2, 120),
              0.435, 0.19, 0.206, 0.16, id_offset = n_per_arm),
  make_cohort(n_per_arm, "150 mg (adolescents)", 150, c(54.7, 12.8, 35, 74.1),
              0.368, 0.21, 0.105, 0, id_offset = 2L * n_per_arm)
)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(unique(events[, c("id", "time", "evid")])))
```

# Simulation

```{r simulate}
sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, events = events, keep = c("cohort")) |>
  as.data.frame()
sim$cohort <- factor(sim$cohort,
  levels = c("150 mg (adults)", "300 mg (adults)", "150 mg (adolescents)"))
```

# Concentration, total TFPI and peak thrombin over time

The paper's Figure 7 overlays the phase III observations on predictions for
adolescents from the earlier phase I/II model, not the model packaged here. The
panels below show the packaged model's median and 90% prediction interval
(individual predictions, no residual error) for each regimen. Observed phase III
values for comparison are steady-state total TFPI of about 100-600 ng/mL (about
3-17 nM), with medians near 300 ng/mL, and peak thrombin of about 30-130 nM with
medians near 55-65 nM (Figure 7C-D).

```{r figure-time-course, fig.height = 7}
sim |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, cohort, Cc, total_target, peak_thrombin) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(Cc, total_target, peak_thrombin), names_to = "output") |>
  dplyr::mutate(output = factor(output,
    levels = c("Cc", "total_target", "peak_thrombin"),
    labels = c("Total marstacimab (ug/mL)", "Total TFPI (nM)", "Peak thrombin (nM)"))) |>
  dplyr::group_by(cohort, output, time) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    q05 = quantile(value, 0.05), q50 = median(value), q95 = quantile(value, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(time / 24, q50)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q05, ymax = q95), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(output ~ cohort, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Time (days)", y = NULL,
       caption = "Median and 5th-95th percentiles of individual predictions, 200 virtual participants per regimen.")
```

# PKNCA validation against Table 7

Table 7 reports steady-state Cmin, Cmax, Cavg and AUC over the 168 h dosing
interval, and the accumulation ratio (AUC over the steady-state interval divided
by AUC over the first interval). The simulation gives 30 weekly doses with no
loading dose, matching Table 7's '150 mg or 300 mg SC QW', and takes the last
interval as steady state.

```{r pknca}
sim_nca <- sim |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, Cc, cohort)
sim_nca <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  sim_nca,
  sim_nca |> dplyr::distinct(id, cohort) |> dplyr::mutate(time = 0, Cc = 0)
) |>
  dplyr::distinct(id, cohort, time, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::arrange(id, cohort, time)

dose_df <- events |>
  dplyr::filter(evid == 1) |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, amt, cohort)

conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(sim_nca, Cc ~ time | cohort + id)
dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_df, amt ~ time | cohort + id)
intervals <- data.frame(
  start = c(0, ss_start),
  end = c(tau, ss_start + tau),
  auclast = TRUE,
  cmin = c(FALSE, TRUE),
  cmax = c(FALSE, TRUE),
  cav = c(FALSE, TRUE)
)
nca_res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals))
nca_df <- as.data.frame(nca_res$result)

ss_long <- nca_df |>
  dplyr::filter(start == ss_start, PPTESTCD %in% c("cmin", "cmax", "cav", "auclast")) |>
  dplyr::select(id, cohort, PPTESTCD, PPORRES)
accumulation <- nca_df |>
  dplyr::filter(PPTESTCD == "auclast") |>
  dplyr::mutate(interval = ifelse(start == 0, "first", "ss")) |>
  dplyr::select(id, cohort, interval, PPORRES) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = interval, values_from = PPORRES) |>
  dplyr::transmute(id, cohort, PPTESTCD = "accumulation", PPORRES = ss / first)
sim_long <- dplyr::bind_rows(ss_long, accumulation) |>
  dplyr::mutate(cohort = as.character(cohort))

# Table 7 medians; concentrations converted from ng/mL to ug/mL
published <- tibble::tribble(
  ~cohort,                ~cmin, ~cmax, ~cav, ~auclast, ~accumulation,
  "150 mg (adults)",      9.40,  13.6,  12.6, 2110,     4.37,
  "300 mg (adults)",      47.3,  57.3,  54.7, 9200,     3.90,
  "150 mg (adolescents)", 28.0,  32.4,  31.3, 5260,     4.46
)

cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = sim_long,
  reference = published,
  by = "cohort",
  units = c(cmin = "ug/mL", cmax = "ug/mL", cav = "ug/mL", auclast = "ug*h/mL"),
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
knitr::kable(cmp,
  caption = "Simulated vs Table 7 medians (AUClast is AUC over the steady-state dosing interval). * differs from the reference by >20%.")
```

```{r pknca-assert}
med_sim <- sim_long |>
  dplyr::group_by(cohort, PPTESTCD) |>
  dplyr::summarise(med = median(PPORRES), .groups = "drop")
med_cav <- setNames(
  med_sim$med[med_sim$PPTESTCD == "cav"],
  med_sim$cohort[med_sim$PPTESTCD == "cav"]
)
ref_cav <- setNames(published$cav, published$cohort)
cav_pct <- 100 * (med_cav[names(ref_cav)] / ref_cav - 1)

stopifnot(
  # Structural: a wrong molecular weight, a missing mg-to-nmol conversion or a
  # mis-transcribed CL / Vmax moves every median by far more than this.
  # Authored at -6% / -15% / -13%; the median of 200 draws has a sampling SE
  # of roughly 7%, so 30% leaves room for any cohort the model can produce.
  all(abs(cav_pct) < 30),
  # Weight scaling: adolescents (median about 55 kg) reach more than twice the
  # adult exposure on the same dose in both the paper and the model.
  med_cav[["150 mg (adolescents)"]] / med_cav[["150 mg (adults)"]] > 1.5
)
```

Steady-state Cmax, Cavg and AUC lie within 15% of the Table 7 medians for all
three regimens, as does Cmin for adults. Adolescent Cmin is 25% lower than
published. Table 7 summarises the 17 adolescents' own empirical Bayes estimates,
while the virtual cohort draws covariates independently from the study
summaries. The accumulation ratio matches for 300 mg but is about 30% lower than
published for both 150 mg regimens. The paper does not say how the first-dose
AUC was obtained for participants who started on a 300 mg loading dose, which
is most of the 150 mg group. A nonlinear model's first-interval AUC also
depends strongly on which dose came first. The accumulation ratio is therefore
reported, not asserted.

The effective half-life follows from the accumulation ratio through
`t1/2 = tau * ln(2) / ln(Rac / (Rac - 1))` (Supplementary eq 9). For the
simulated median Rac of the 150 mg adult regimen,
`r round(med_sim$med[med_sim$cohort == "150 mg (adults)" & med_sim$PPTESTCD == "accumulation"], 2)`,
this gives
`r round(tau * log(2) / log((function(r) r / (r - 1))(med_sim$med[med_sim$cohort == "150 mg (adults)" & med_sim$PPTESTCD == "accumulation"])) / 24, 1)`
days. The paper reports a median of 18.7 days; the gap follows directly from
the lower accumulation ratio discussed above.

# Assumptions and deviations

- **Weight exponents on Q and Vp.** The Methods, the Fig. 1 caption and the EMA
  assessment report (EMA/464842/2024) all state that weight enters CL, Vc, Q
  and Vp. Table 5 and the base-model Table S3 report only two exponents, 1.14
  on CL and 1.86 on Vc. The maintainers pair Q with the CL exponent and Vp with
  the Vc exponent, the usual clearance-type / volume-type pairing; the paper
  does not say which exponent Q and Vp used. The authors have been asked.
- **Molecular weight.** Converting mg doses to nmol (Vmax, Km and KSS are in nM)
  needs the antibody's molecular weight, which the paper does not state. The
  model uses the 146 kDa of the Hympavzi US prescribing information
  (section 11). Total marstacimab is returned as `Cc` in ug/mL; total TFPI
  (`total_target`), free TFPI (`free_target`) and peak thrombin are in nM.
- **KSS units.** Table 5 prints KSS without a unit; it is taken as nM, the
  concentration unit of the TMDD system (Km, Vmax and baseline TFPI are all
  in nM).
- **Healthy-volunteer and hemophilia-type coding.** The reference population is
  hemophilia A (Table 5 footnote). Healthy volunteers take `DIS_HEALTHY = 1`
  and `DIS_HEMOPHILIA_B = 0`, so the two linear effects never apply together.
  Native Hawaiian participants, listed separately in Table 4, are non-Asian
  (`RACE_ASIAN = 0`). Mild renal impairment is eGFR below 90 mL/min/1.73 m^2;
  the data set had no moderate or severe impairment.
- **Bioavailability IIV.** Supplementary eq 1 places exponential IIV on F, as
  on every other parameter, so an individual F can exceed 1. This happens for
  about 3% of draws (variance 0.0332 around 0.705). The model reproduces the
  paper's form without truncation.
- **Peak thrombin applies to hemophilia.** The Emax model was fitted to
  participants with hemophilia only (Methods, 'Emax PK/PD Model'). The model
  computes `peak_thrombin` for any participant, but for healthy volunteers it is
  an extrapolation.
- **Figure 4 plateaus.** The curve printed in Figure 4 levels off near 40 nM
  and 94 nM, about 4% above Table 8's PBASE (37.8 nM) and PMAX (91.4 nM), while
  its midpoint matches EC50. The model uses the Table 8 values.
- **Injection site.** The secondary injection-site analysis (Table S6: F
  multiplied by 0.951 for the arm and 0.959 for the thigh, with the other
  parameters fixed) is a separate re-fit and is not part of the packaged model.
- **Accumulation ratio for 150 mg QW.** The simulated median accumulation
  ratio (about 3) and the effective half-life derived from it fall about 30%
  below Table 7 (4.37 for adults and 4.46 for adolescents), although the
  steady-state exposure matches. The parameters were not adjusted.
- **Virtual cohort.** Covariates are drawn independently from the Table 3 and
  Table 4 summaries; the paper's Table 7 uses the participants' own empirical
  Bayes estimates, so medians can differ by more than sampling error.
- Europe PMC listed no erratum or correction notice for this article (PMID
  42698050) as of 2026-11-23.
